suites.label: Core runtime regression
suites.purpose: Did a change to the iii Engine, its workers or the Harness break a core capability agents rely on every day? Thirteen short tasks each exercise one capability: updating saved state, switching to a replaced function, waking on a timer, editing and testing code with the shell and coder workers, database migrations in transactions, parallel agents writing to one table, validators that reject a turn, long sessions that read more than the agent can keep verbatim, instructions hidden in tool output, delegation that stops at the sub-agent depth cap, the Harness refusing to re-run a call that keeps failing or to run one cut short by the output limit, and a session and a held turn surviving restarts of session-manager and the Harness, run last. The two call guards depend on the model provoking them; a run where it did not is undetermined, not scored. Not covered: whole applications, Console pages, browsers, Workers started by Compose and multi-hour work (see Application builds and changes, and Linkly).

suites.label: Application builds and changes
suites.purpose: Can an agent running on iii build and change real software end to end, and does it still work when an independent checker runs it? The suite has a seven-chapter Kanban app (iii functions, Compose, browser); a feature in iii's own Registry, then an independent check of that delivery by a second agent; a website built from a written spec; Alertmanager's Go routing moved into an iii function; and three Workers with their own Console pages (chess, issue form, CI simulator). Not covered: isolated runtime primitives (Core runtime regression) and Registry planning or environment setup, which run only as diagnostics.

suites.label: Application builds with Deepwork
suites.purpose: Can Deepwork delegate the implementation and verification of real Workers and deliver working Console applications? Runs the existing chess, form-flow and state-machine build contracts on the deepwork stack with the deepwork-e2e profile. This suite exercises the plain flow, without Git worktrees or interactive approval.

suites.label: Build Linkly from the tutorial
suites.purpose: Does the agentic tutorial we point users to still work? One long session builds the Linkly link shortener on a fresh linkly-agentic scaffold, chapter by chapter, adding workers through Compose. It then checks that a request to restart the whole project is refused. Not covered: other templates or tutorials. The seven chapters are one test with one score, so the result does not say which chapter broke unless you open the criteria.

suites.label: Complete the onboarding tour
suites.purpose: Can a new user still finish the onboarding we hand them? One session on a fresh harness project with the tour's worker, as iii project init --learn-iii creates it, sends each tour step's prompt under the harness template's Onboarding profile: say hello, add a database, list what the system can do, build a reactive TODO worker with a Console page, then remove the tour. The test plays the tour page: it closes the button steps, closes each agent step when its trigger fires, and checks the TODO items off as the user would. Not covered: the setup wizard and the tour's on-screen guidance (the page, the spotlight and the panels it opens).

suites.label: Essential checks before merge
suites.purpose: Before merging a change to iii, do the four most basic agent paths still work? The four paths: one exact state write at minimal cost, a safe update of saved data, adapting to a replaced function, and fixing code with the shell and coder workers. Not covered: timers, subagents, databases, validators, long context and prompt injection (all in Core runtime regression), and anything visual.

suites.label: Published stack checks
suites.purpose: Run five checks on the published stack: one precise state write, state persistence, adapting to a changed tool contract, repairing Python code, and timer wake-ups.

suites.label: Application builds and changes ×3 (weekly)
suites.purpose: Once a week, the tests of Application builds and changes run three independent times on the same stack, to measure how much that suite's results vary when nothing changed.

suites.label: Application builds and changes ×9 (harness comparison)
suites.purpose: To compare two Harness versions, all 14 cases of Application builds and changes run nine independent times on each, enough to rule out a quality drop of more than 5 points once failures that are not the Harness's are set aside. Decided on 2026-10-24: run on demand when a Harness release is judged, about US$45 a comparison for both arms on deepseek-flash, within a ceiling of about US$50 together with regression-x11. Dispatch it once per arm, on the pair of stacks in stacks/harness-ab/.

suites.label: Null agent canary
suites.purpose: Proves that no Core runtime regression test, nor the minimal state write, gives points or a completion to an agent that does nothing: run with the null-agent profile, which answers done and calls no function, every test must score 0 and stay incomplete, and any point or completion is a hole in that test's evaluator.

suites.label: Core runtime regression ×11 (harness comparison)
suites.purpose: To compare two Harness versions, the thirteen Core runtime regression tests run eleven independent times on each, enough to rule out a quality drop of more than 5 points once failures that are not the Harness's are set aside. Decided on 2026-10-24: run on demand when a Harness release is judged, about US$3 a comparison for both arms on deepseek-flash, within a ceiling of about US$50 together with software-engineering-x9. Dispatch it once per arm, on the pair of stacks in stacks/harness-ab/.

suites.label: Context capacity (compaction)
suites.purpose: Does the Harness manage its context when the window is small? Four tests that already exist run on the context-capacity stack, which cuts the usable window of the model to about 128 thousand tokens, so long sessions cross it and the context manager has to compact: Kanban chapters 1, 4 and 7 and the long-session context pressure test. Not covered: the order of magnitude of a normal window, and what happens after a compaction beyond what these tests check. Scores here are not comparable with the same tests in a normal window; read them only against other runs of this suite.

suites.label: Human approval of agent calls
suites.purpose: Does a call held for a human still run exactly once when approved and never when denied? Runs on stacks/approvals.yaml, the default stack plus the approval gate, which holds every call of every session for approval; that is why it cannot join a suite on the default stack. The runner plays the human: it allows a release, denies a purge, and checks that no pending approval is left behind. Not covered: the Console's approval inbox, auto mode and always-allow rules, and filesystem-access approvals.

suites.label: Memory quality
suites.purpose: For every memory release, does the memory worker put the right stored facts in front of a live session, once and without unrelated padding, and does a session with memory do better than one without?

suites.label: Memory learning
suites.purpose: Does memory learn what the user says in a chat, and only from the user? Before the measured session, a teacher session of the user's own kind states a fact, an instruction or a correction; memory's extraction must keep it, and the later session must get it and use it. A deploy key said in passing must never be stored, injected or answered, and a non-user (test or automation) session asking memory to remember must teach it nothing. A fact in the middle of a long message must be learned like one at its start, and a standing rule against remembering the user's health must keep a diagnosis out of the bank, beside a control without the rule that shows extraction would keep it. Extraction calls a model, so these gates move with that model, unlike the memory suite's; the fact and instruction cases compare with the memory suite's baselines. Not covered: what a sub-agent teaches, and learning into a bank other than the session's.
